summary: This experimental memo presents a specification for version 7 of the Internet Protocol, along with version 7 of TCP and UDP, as a proposed successor to the existing protocols. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6814.

eli5.summary: This paper imagines a whole new version of the main Internet rules. It was one of several ideas that did not take off. It is historic.

questions: how does ipv7 addressing differ from ipv4
subtitle: A proposed Internet Protocol version 7 with 64-bit addresses and improved routing.

tldr.problem: IPv4 faced three critical problems: exhausting 32-bit addresses, routing explosion from flat network assignment, and TCP limitations at high bandwidth and long latencies.
tldr.mechanism: TP/IX defines version 7 of IP, TCP, and UDP with 64-bit addresses split into administrative domains and networks, expanded port numbers, and a forward route identifier field to support fast flow-based forwarding while maintaining backward compatibility with IPv4 where possible.
tldr.outcome: This experimental proposal was one of several visions for the next generation of Internet protocols, but did not prevail. The Internet eventually adopted IPv6. RFC 6814 superseded this specification.

today: RFC 1475 is Historic. TP/IX was one of several competing proposals for the next generation of Internet protocols in the early 1990s, including TUBA, PIP, and others. The Internet Engineering Task Force eventually selected a different direction, developing IPv6 instead. RFC 6814 superseded this specification.

sections.title: Problems and Objectives
sections.content:
RFC 1475 addresses three major scaling problems IPv4 faced by 1993. First, the 32-bit address space was too small, especially as microprocessors were being deployed in unexpected places like embedded devices. Second, routing architectures were breaking down because assigning network numbers to every organization created a flat, unscalable routing table. Third, TCP itself was becoming a bottleneck at gigabit speeds and on long international links, limited by 16-bit ports, 32-bit sequence numbers, and 16-bit window size.

The author's design objectives were to learn from IPv4, retain its "look and feel", avoid hard-coded routing information in addresses (unlike IPv4 classes), allow hosts to upgrade independently without a global transition plan, and permit stateless translation between IPv4 and IPv7.
sections.eli5: Three things about IPv4 were running out: the address numbers, the routing scheme, and the speed limits on fast networks. This proposal tries to fix all three at once.

sections.title: The 64-Bit Address and Administrative Hierarchy
sections.content:
TP/IX expands addresses from 32 to 64 bits, structured as Administrative Domain (AD) (24 bits), Network (24 bits), and Host (16 bits). ADs are allocated downward from 192 in the IPv4 class A space initially, providing for over 2 million administrative domains—enough for service providers, national authorities, and large organizations. Most routing happens on the full 48-bit AD+Network number, allowing aggregation without fixed hierarchical coupling to routing like IPv4 classes caused.

The RFC argues 64 bits is sufficient: 32 bits of addresses for every computer on Earth, and 32 more bits for every byte of storage. Existing IPv4 addresses are mapped into the NSF AD (number 192.0.0), allowing both IPv4 and IPv7 addresses to coexist during transition.
sections.eli5: The new address is really four parts: an admin area, a network, and a host, with plenty of room for growth. Old IPv4 addresses get fitted into the new system automatically.

sections.title: IPv7 Header, TCP, and UDP Changes
sections.content:
The TP/IX IP header expands addresses to 64 bits but remains simpler than IPv4 in other ways. The Version field is 4 bits (set to 7), Header Length is 12 bits allowing headers up to 16,380 bytes. The Time To Live field expands to 16 bits (nominally in 1/16-second units) to support faster networks and longer paths. A new Forward Route Identifier field (64 bits) carries routing information from one hop to the next, enabling extremely fast path-based forwarding.

TCP expands its port numbers to 32 bits (allowing 4 billion ports), sequence and acknowledgement numbers to 64 bits (supporting gigabit speeds), and window size to 32 bits. UDP similarly expands its ports to 32 bits. Both reduce the port exhaustion problem that plagued IPv4 at high transaction rates.
sections.eli5: The new headers have bigger numbers for addresses, ports, and sequence numbers so they don't run out at high speeds or on fast networks.

sections.title: Forward Route Identifier and Fast Forwarding
sections.content:
A key innovation is the Forward Route Identifier (FRI)—a 64-bit opaque field that each router updates based on its own routing table. When a router has routing information for a destination, it fills in an identifier that the next hop can use directly to make its own forwarding decision without a table lookup. This avoids routing table searches for subsequent hops on the same path.

The scheme supports flows and tunnels: if a flow is set up, the FRI contains a flow identifier instead of a route identifier. For mobile hosts, host routes can propagate as targeted routes in the routing protocol (RAP), and the FRI acts as an effective tunnel to the mobile host's current location, enabling transparent mobility without address changes.
sections.eli5: Each router stamps the packet with a shortcut for the next router to find the right path fast, instead of making every router search its big table.

sections.title: IPv4 to IPv7 Conversion and Coexistence
sections.content:
TP/IX defines stateless translation of datagrams between IPv4 and IPv7, allowing the two protocols to coexist during a long transition. IPv4 hosts need not change; an IPv7 option can carry the original IPv4 address for reassembly on the return path. IPv7 hosts implement a "Don't Convert" option to prohibit conversion, and TCP's 32-bit rollover option handles sequence number conversion for TCP/IPv4 hosts that encounter IPv7 intermediaries.

The RFC emphasizes that IPv4 hosts should be able to continue operating indefinitely within their own organization, with translation at boundaries. No site is forced to upgrade; hosts and routers can upgrade at random, with no global transition plan constraint. Eventually subnet routers must implement IPv7 routing when IPv7 host numbers are no longer globally unique, but that can happen gradually.
sections.eli5: Old IPv4 networks can keep working unchanged, and new IPv7 networks can grow alongside them. Special routers translate between them so everyone can talk to everyone else.

sections.title: Design Philosophy and Status
sections.content:
The RFC reflects a philosophy that protocols should become simpler as they evolve. Rather than inheriting IPv4 complexity, TP/IX removes fields not universally needed (options are not required to be implemented, only understood; implementations must understand option classes but need not implement specific options). The author emphasizes learning from IPv4's mistakes—notably the fixed class system that became the protocol's worst problem—by avoiding hard-coded routing structures.

The RFC notes a small section on ICMP conversion and domains, and discusses the relative merits of path-based vs. hop-by-hop forwarding, concluding that TP/IX supports both through its design. The specification is complete but intentionally forward-thinking, allowing future allocation of address space and evolution of option definitions without breaking deployed systems.
sections.eli5: The protocol tries to be smarter than IPv4 by learning what worked and what didn't, and by leaving room for ideas not even invented yet.

fields.name: Header Length
fields.desc: Count of 32-bit words in header; max 16,380 bytes.

fields.name: Time To Live
fields.desc: Nominally in 1/16-second units; decremented by at least 1 per hop.

fields.name: Total Datagram Length
fields.desc: Length of entire datagram in octets; up to 4.3 GB.

fields.name: Forward Route Identifier
fields.desc: Opaque routing hint for next hop to expedite forwarding.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: 16-bit one's complement checksum of IP header.
